results.result: C. elegans locomotion is driven by multiple, separate oscillators: forward locomotion involves head oscillations and B-MN-driven body oscillations, while backward locomotion involves A-MN-driven body oscillations. The persistence of head oscillations after ablation of premotor INs or ventral cord MNs indicates separation of head and body oscillators.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C45, C127, C130-C132 collectively demonstrate through ablation experiments (C38-C47) that head oscillations persist when either premotor INs or MNs are ablated, indicating separate oscillators. The behavioral data (Figures 1-2) showing differential effects of ablating different neuron classes strongly support the existence of multiple, functionally distinct oscillators for forward and backward locomotion.

results.result: A-class motor neurons exhibit intrinsic oscillatory activity sufficient to drive backward locomotion without premotor interneurons. When premotor INs and B-MNs are removed, animals exhibit predominantly backward locomotion with robust body bending, indicating A-MNs function as both motor executors and rhythm generators.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C47, C51-C53, C125, C128, C162 are strongly supported by converging evidence from ablation experiments (C48-C50, Figure 2), electrophysiology showing periodic rPSC bursts (C63-C64, C66, Figure 4), and calcium imaging revealing robust oscillations in A-MNs after premotor IN/B-MN ablation (C73-C75, Figure 4D-H). The behavioral data showing organized backward locomotion without premotor INs (C52-C53) directly supports the sufficiency claim.

results.result: A-MNs function as a distributed chain of phase-coupled local oscillators. Sparse ablation of A-MNs in different body regions alters but does not abolish backward locomotion, with rhythmic bending arising from multiple locations and local wave speed decreasing only in ablated regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60, C185 are well-supported by systematic regional ablation experiments (Figure 3) showing that removal of anterior, mid-body, or posterior A-MNs causes local defects but allows bending initiation from other regions (C54, C58). The quantitative analysis (C59, Figure 3D) demonstrates localized effects on wave speed, and the observation of independent head/tail oscillations (C55-C57) supports the distributed oscillator model.

results.result: A-MNs generate periodic electrical activities without premotor INs, as evidenced by rhythmic PSC bursts observed in 70% of preparations after premotor IN and B-MN ablation. These rPSC bursts occur at ~90s intervals with distinct characteristics (2-3s duration, 3-10 Hz, -50 to -300 pA), and are largely abolished when A-MNs are removed.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C70 are supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—supplement 1) showing periodic rPSC bursts after ablation that are distinct from baseline mPSCs. The specificity to A-MNs is confirmed by the 60% reduction in mPSC frequency and loss of periodic bursts when A-MNs are ablated (C70). The correspondence with action potential bursts (C68) and muscle contraction (C69) supports physiological relevance.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of A-MNs, but not B-MNs, exhibits rPSC bursts at intermediate light intensities, while high intensity stimulation of both produces high-frequency PSCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by optogenetic experiments (Figure 4—supplement 2) showing differential responses of A-MNs versus B-MNs to graded light stimulation. The emergence of rPSC bursts specifically in A-MNs at intermediate intensities provides additional evidence for their intrinsic oscillatory properties.

results.result: Calcium imaging reveals robust oscillations in A-MNs after co-ablation of premotor INs and B-MNs. Individual A-MNs share a ~50s oscillatory cycle with variable amplitudes, exhibit phase relationships consistent with muscle activation patterns (dorsal vs. ventral, anterior vs. posterior), and show oscillation frequency positively correlated with crawling speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C79 are well-supported by calcium imaging data (Figures 4D-H, 5). The observation of robust oscillations in all animals after ablation (C73), shared oscillatory cycle (C74), highest activity in DA9 (C75), appropriate phase relationships (C76-C78), and correlation with speed (C79) provide comprehensive evidence for organized A-MN oscillatory activity. The simultaneous imaging of multiple A-MNs (Figure 5) directly demonstrates coordinated activity.

results.result: The UNC-2 P/Q/N-type high-voltage-activated calcium channel underlies A-MN oscillation. Loss-of-function mutations in unc-2 and its auxiliary subunits (unc-36, calf-1) abolish evoked and endogenous rPSC bursts and severely reduce DA9 calcium oscillation amplitude and frequency, while mutations in L-type VGCC or sodium leak channels do not affect rPSC bursts. A-MN-specific restoration of UNC-2 rescues oscillation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C88-C97, C142 are strongly supported by comprehensive genetic analysis (Figure 7, Figure 7—supplements 1-2). The specific requirement for P/Q/N-type VGCC components (C91-C92) versus other channels (C88-C90), loss of both evoked and endogenous bursts in unc-2(lf) (C94-C95), cell-autonomous rescue (C96), and persistence of oscillations in unc-13(lf) (C98) collectively demonstrate that UNC-2 functions in membrane oscillation independent of its exocytosis role (C97).

results.result: In unc-13 loss-of-function mutants that lack chemical synaptic transmission, DA9 exhibits periodic calcium oscillations after premotor IN and B-MN ablation, similar to wildtype animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by calcium imaging in unc-13(lf) mutants (Figure 7G-I) showing maintained oscillations despite loss of chemical transmission. This result, combined with the established role of UNC-13 in exocytosis (C99), provides strong evidence that A-MN oscillation is independent of chemical synaptic input and exocytosis.

results.result: UNC-2 localizes to both presynaptic termini along neuronal processes and to punctate sites on neuron somata, including A-MN somata, as shown by endogenous GFP tagging.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by imaging of endogenous GFP::UNC-2 (Figure 8E) showing somatic localization in addition to the expected presynaptic localization. This anatomical evidence is consistent with UNC-2's proposed role in somatic membrane oscillation.

results.result: Bidirectional manipulation of UNC-2 activity produces corresponding changes in A-MN oscillation and backward locomotion. Loss-of-function unc-2 mutants show reduced rPSC bursts, DA9 oscillation, reversal velocity, and backward propensity, while gain-of-function mutants show increased values. A-MN-specific rescue is sufficient to restore oscillation.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C108 are strongly supported by comprehensive analysis of unc-2(lf) and unc-2(gf) mutants (Figures 7-8) showing bidirectional effects on electrophysiology (C101-C104), calcium imaging (C102, C104), and behavior (C106-C107). The cell-autonomous rescue (C105) and correlation between oscillatory properties and locomotion (C108) provide strong evidence for UNC-2's causal role in A-MN oscillation and backward locomotion.

results.result: Descending premotor interneurons AVA regulate A-MN activity through a mixed gap junction and chemical synapse configuration. Optogenetic AVA stimulation induces rPSC bursts with similar characteristics to endogenous A-MN bursts, and these evoked bursts are abolished when A-MNs but not B-MNs are removed, indicating AVA potentiates A-MN intrinsic oscillation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C81-C87, C129 are well-supported by optogenetic experiments (Figure 6) showing AVA-evoked rPSC bursts with similar properties to endogenous bursts (C83), specific requirement for A-MNs (C84-C85), and the inference that AVA potentiates rather than generates the oscillation (C86-C87). The anatomical basis (C81) is established by prior work.

results.result: At rest, AVA-A gap junctions inhibit A-MN intrinsic oscillation via UNC-7 innexin. DA9 shows low calcium activity in wildtype and unc-13(lf) mutants (where AVA-A coupling is intact) but robust oscillation in unc-7(lf) mutants. AVA-specific UNC-7 rescue dampens DA9 oscillation. When premotor INs and B-MNs are ablated, robust oscillations occur across all genotypes, confirming A-MN intrinsic oscillatory property is unaltered by unc-7 mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C116, C181 are strongly supported by experiments in unc-7(lf) mutants (Figure 9D-F, Figure 9—supplement 1) showing that loss of gap junctions releases A-MN oscillation (C112), AVA-specific rescue restores inhibition (C113), and ablation reveals intact intrinsic oscillatory capacity (C114-C115). The contrast with unc-13(lf) (C111) demonstrates the specific role of gap junctions versus chemical synapses.

results.result: AVA exerts state-dependent dual regulation of A-MN activity and the reversal motor state. At rest, unc-7 mutants display kinker posture and increased spontaneous reversals; AVA-specific UNC-7 rescue inhibits spontaneous reversals and restores forward bias. Upon activation, AVA potentiates A-MNs primarily through chemical synapses (normal rPSC frequency in unc-7, abolished in unc-13). After premotor IN/B-MN ablation, unc-7 mutants exhibit continuous backward locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C124 are well-supported by behavioral analysis of unc-7 mutants (Figure 9G-I, Figure 9—supplement 1D) and electrophysiology (Figure 9A-C). The rescue of spontaneous reversal phenotype by AVA-specific UNC-7 (C118), maintained AVA-evoked rPSCs in unc-7 but not unc-13 (C121-C123), and continuous reversals after ablation (C120) collectively support the dual regulation model (C124).

results.result: Positive and negative regulation of A-MN oscillatory activity, through manipulation of UNC-2 or AVA synaptic inputs, leads to changes in the propensity, velocity, and duration of the reversal motor state.
results.evaluation: Claim C126 is supported by the collective evidence from UNC-2 manipulation (C106-C108, Figure 8) and AVA regulation experiments (C117-C124, Figure 9), demonstrating that modulating A-MN oscillatory activity through different mechanisms produces corresponding changes in reversal behavior.

results.result: Ablation of premotor INs or A/B/D-MNs produces distinct motor phenotypes. Animals without premotor INs exhibit reduced motility but retain locomotor activity with a kinker-like posture (head oscillates, body bends disorganized) and robust muscle activity. Animals without A/B/D-MNs show attenuated body bending with persistent head oscillation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C44 are supported by behavioral analysis and calcium imaging (Figure 1, Video 1) showing distinct phenotypes after different ablations. The kinker posture (C39), retained muscle activity (C41), and anatomical explanation for attenuated bending (C44) are well-documented.

results.result: Selective ablation of different MN classes in premotor IN-less animals reveals distinct motor outputs: removal of A-MNs produces sluggish forward locomotion, removal of B-MNs produces backward locomotion with robust bending, and removal of D-MNs maintains kinker-like posture.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by systematic ablation experiments (Figure 2, Video 2) showing differential effects of removing specific MN classes. The behavioral phenotypes are clearly distinct and support the inference that A-MNs drive body bends in the absence of premotor INs.

results.result: The difference in frequency between A-MN-dependent rPSC bursts in dissected preparations (~90s intervals) and A-MN calcium oscillation in immobilized (~50s) versus crawling C. elegans may reflect the effect of motor and proprioceptive feedback.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While the frequency differences are documented (C63, C74, C79), the proposed explanation involving proprioceptive feedback is not directly tested. Additional experiments manipulating proprioception would be needed to support this interpretation.

results.result: Separating forward- and reversal-driving oscillators at the motor neuron level offers a different strategy for directional movements compared to lamprey and Drosophila. In the absence of premotor INs, C. elegans generates deeper body bends during backward than forward locomotion, suggesting reversal-driving A-MNs have intrinsically higher activity than forward-promoting B-MNs. This requires AVA to attenuate A-MN activity through electrical coupling to establish forward movement as the preferred motor state.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C137 are supported by the collective experimental evidence showing separate oscillators (C1, C127-C132), differential bending depth (C135, observed in Figures 1-2), and AVA-mediated inhibition (C109-C116, C181). The comparison to other systems (C134) is based on established knowledge. Claim C138 is speculative but logically follows from the data.

results.result: This study describes the first example of motor neurons performing both motor and rhythm-generating roles in a locomotor circuit, bearing resemblance to the lobster pyloric circuit where pyloric MNs are capable of intrinsic oscillation and bursting.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 are supported by the comprehensive evidence for A-MN oscillatory activity (C2-C3, C125, C128) and the comparison to established knowledge about other systems (C139, C141). The novelty claim (C140) is justified by the demonstration that A-MNs both execute movement and generate rhythm.

results.result: An exocytosis-independent role of high-voltage-activated calcium channels in membrane oscillation has been noted in vertebrates, including lamprey spinal neurons and rat pedunculopontine nucleus. Voltage-activated calcium conductance may be a shared property of neurons with oscillatory activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C146 are supported by citations to established literature (C144-C145) and the current study's findings (C97, C142). The speculation that this is a shared property (C146) is reasonable given the cross-species evidence, though it remains a hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: The C. elegans locomotor network utilizes a combinatory oscillatory and bursting property of MNs and muscles to generate motor rhythm. Despite lacking voltage-activated sodium channels and having non-spiking neurons, C. elegans MNs exhibit calcium oscillations and muscles fire calcium-driven action potentials. A-MNs are required for muscle bursting, and altering A-MN oscillation changes bursting frequency and duration. High-voltage-activated calcium channels (UNC-2 P/Q/N- and L-type VGCCs) take deterministic roles in rhythmic output.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C156 are supported by the current study's findings (C2-C4, C150, C153-C154) combined with established knowledge about C. elegans neurobiology (C147-C149, C151-C152). The proposal (C155-C156) integrates these findings into a coherent model explaining how C. elegans generates motor rhythm without classic action potentials.

results.result: C. elegans motor infrastructure exhibits functional compression: despite operating with remarkably few neurons, it shows remarkable behavioral adaptability by compressing multiple functions into fewer cells and layers. Body wall muscles are the only bursting cells, excitatory MNs absorb the role of rhythm generators and are likely proprioceptive, performing all essential functions of large locomotor CPG networks. This compression may be necessitated by anatomical constraints, with cellular complexity compensating for numeric simplicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C167 are supported by the current study's findings (C2-C3, C128, C162) combined with established knowledge (C157-C159) and anatomical considerations (C164). The compression concept (C160, C166-C167) is well-supported by the demonstration that A-MNs perform multiple functions (rhythm generation, motor execution, likely proprioception C163). Claims C165-C167 involve some speculation but are logically grounded in the data.

results.result: Mixed chemical and electrical synaptic connectivity between INs and MNs may be a universal feature of rhythm-generating circuits, found in crayfish, leech, C. elegans, Drosophila, zebrafish, and other motor systems. In C. elegans, this configuration allows AVA to exert state-dependent inhibition (via gap junctions at rest) and activation (via chemical synapses when stimulated) of A-MN oscillatory activity. C. elegans innexin mutants permit direct behavioral assessment of gap junction roles, revealing sophisticated functions of this mixed synapse configuration.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C183 are supported by the current study's findings on AVA-A regulation (C5-C6, C109-C124, C180-C182) combined with extensive citations to established knowledge about mixed synapses in other systems (C169-C176). The behavioral analysis in unc-7 mutants (C178-C179) provides direct evidence for the sophisticated roles of this configuration. Claim C183 is speculative but supported by prior work.

results.result: In the reversal-promoting circuit, proprioception may serve as feedback to regulate A-MN oscillation and organize phasic relationships, with A-MNs potentially integrating the roles of rhythm-generating and proprioceptive INs. DA9, the most posterior unit with highest activity, may be a leading oscillator, analogous to the fastest oscillator in lamprey spinal cord that entrains others.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C190 involve significant speculation (C187-C188, C190 marked as SPECULATION). While C186 is supported by citation and C189 by established knowledge, the proposed role of proprioception in A-MN coordination (C187-C188) and DA9 as leading oscillator (C190) are reasonable hypotheses based on the data (C75, C79) but require direct experimental testing. The phase relationships (C76-C78) support organized activity but don't definitively establish the mechanism.

results.result: Small animals can solve similar challenges in organizing locomotor behaviors as larger animals, with a conserved molecular repertoire and far fewer neurons. They serve as compact models to dissect organizational logics of neural circuits, where all essential functions are instantiated but compressed into fewer layers and cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C191-C192 are supported by the comprehensive findings of the study demonstrating that C. elegans achieves complex locomotor control with minimal neurons by compressing functions (C8, C160-C167). The conservation of molecular components (UNC-2, mixed synapses) and circuit principles across species supports this conclusion.
